name: Vision therapy (behavioral optometry)

card.summary: A supervised program of eye exercises and lens or prism activities used to train eye teaming and focusing, and sometimes to improve eye alignment so the eyes look straighter and more comfortable.
card.aka: Optometric vision therapy, orthoptics, eye exercises
card.note: Research is strongest for convergence insufficiency; broader claims (learning, myopia) are disputed between optometric and medical bodies.

quick.overview:
Vision therapy is a course of individualized eye exercises, often with lenses, prisms, filters or computer games, prescribed after an eye exam. Its goal is better eye teaming, focusing and tracking. For appearance, the relevant payoff is mostly in eye alignment: eyes that turn in or out (strabismus, intermittent exotropia) look misaligned, and therapy aims to steady binocular control so the gaze looks straighter and eyestrain eases.

Randomized trials, including the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial, found office-based therapy helped convergence insufficiency more than placebo therapy or home pencil push-ups [1]. Broader claims, such as treating learning problems or reducing nearsightedness, are disputed: optometric groups support non-strabismic therapy, while ophthalmology and pediatric bodies have called its behavioral aspects unproven.
quick.how: Programs usually combine weekly in-office sessions of 30 to 60 minutes with short daily home exercises such as Brock string work, over roughly three months or longer. Tools include prisms, lenses, red-green glasses, occluders and computer or virtual-reality games. Do-it-yourself eye exercise routines promoted online borrow some of these ideas.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild (temporary headache, eye fatigue, dizziness during exercises). Cost and time commitment are the main downsides, and sessions are often not covered by insurance. Strabismus and amblyopia warrant a medical eye exam first, since some causes need other treatment. Exercises have not been shown to change refractive error such as myopia.

lead: Vision therapy, also called behavioral optometry or optometric vision therapy, is a structured program of eye exercises and activities, supervised by an optometrist or orthoptist, that aims to improve how the two eyes align, focus and track together [13]. Unlike glasses, which compensate for optics, it trains the visual system's motor and sensory skills.

Its link to appearance runs mainly through eye alignment and comfort. Conditions such as convergence insufficiency, intermittent exotropia and some strabismus cause eyes to drift apart or turn, which can be visible in photos and conversation. Therapy aims to improve binocular control so the eyes hold a straighter position and the strain, squinting and tired look that accompany focusing problems are reduced. Online eye-exercise communities also pursue it hoping to sharpen vision or remove glasses, a use that goes beyond what trials have tested.

Controlled research is strongest for convergence insufficiency. A 2005 randomized trial in children found office-based vision therapy outperformed placebo therapy and home pencil push-ups [1], and a companion trial in young adults compared therapy with pencil push-ups [2]. Binocular, game-based approaches for amblyopia and a virtual-reality program for intermittent exotropia have also been trialled [3][4]. Professional bodies differ on the broader field: optometric organizations support it for non-strabismic problems, while ophthalmology, orthoptic and pediatric groups state that the behavioral claims, including learning disability treatment, lack documented evidence [5].

angle.text: For people whose eyes drift or turn, therapy aims to improve how well the eyes hold alignment together, which can make the eyes look straighter and relieve strain-related squinting. Some users also try eye exercises hoping to improve sharpness or reduce glasses reliance, which is a claimed rather than studied outcome.

paras: Programs begin with a comprehensive eye examination to identify specific visual deficits, then combine office sessions with prescribed home activities. Typical targets are eye tracking, focusing (accommodation) and eye teaming (vergence) [13]. Tools include prisms, lenses, filters, occluders and, more recently, computer and virtual-reality games [13][3].

Non-surgical exercises for misaligned eyes were introduced in the late nineteenth century, and the field known as orthoptics developed through the early twentieth. In 1928 A. M. Skeffington co-founded the Optometric Extension Program and is often called the father of behavioral optometry, which framed vision as a broader behavioral process [5][13]. Optometrists later applied training to reading-related eye problems and eye strain [5].

Practitioners use therapy for convergence insufficiency, amblyopia, strabismus, accommodative disorders and vision problems after concussion or brain injury [13][6][7]. A wider set of claims, including help with reading, dyslexia, attention, sports performance and myopia, is promoted by some practitioners and online eye-exercise communities [5].

Misaligned eyes can be visible to others. Therapy for intermittent exotropia and strabismus aims at steadier control of alignment [4], and orthoptic exercise is sometimes used alongside or instead of surgery [13].

A 2005 randomized multicenter trial of 47 children aged 9 to 18 with symptomatic convergence insufficiency compared 12 weeks of office-based therapy, office-based placebo therapy and home pencil push-ups [1]. A parallel trial compared office therapy with pencil push-ups in young adults [2], and a later imaging study measured brain responses in adults with convergence insufficiency after therapy [8].

For amblyopia, reviews describe binocular therapy as a possible adjunct or alternative to patching [9], and a randomized trial of 40 participants tested a video-game platform against patching [3]. A 2026 randomized trial studied virtual-reality vision therapy for intermittent exotropia [4]. After concussion, a randomized trial examined Brock string therapy for a receded near point of convergence [10], and occupational therapy guidelines list vision therapy among supported interventions for brain injury [11].

Studies of non-strabismic therapy for learning have been small, and professional bodies disagree about them (see below). A 2014 randomized trial compared different orthoptic exercise regimes in typical young adults [12].

The American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus have stated that learning disabilities are not caused or treated by visual methods, and AAPOS in 2020 described the behavioral aspects of vision therapy as scientifically unproven [5]. Optometric organizations including the American Optometric Association and the College of Optometrists in Vision Development state that therapy addresses visual problems that can affect learning without directly treating learning disorders [5]. Reviews cited on Wikipedia reached differing conclusions, with one 2008 review finding convergence insufficiency the clearest supported use [5].

Programs of general eye exercises have been promoted for improving nearsightedness. Practitioner sources note that eye exercises have no proven effect on refractive errors such as myopia [13]. China's national school eye exercise program, introduced in 1963, has been discussed in this context because nearsightedness rose over the same period [5].

Reported effects are generally mild, such as temporary eyestrain or headache during exercises. Therapy requires repeated visits and daily home practice, and costs are often not covered by insurance. Conditions such as amblyopia and strabismus require a medical eye examination because other treatments may apply [9].

timeline.event: Louis Emile Javal develops non-surgical exercises for strabismus, an early orthoptic approach [13].
A. M. Skeffington co-founds the Optometric Extension Program [5].
China introduces compulsory school eye exercises for ages 6 to 17 [5].
Randomized trials compare vision therapy with pencil push-ups and placebo therapy for convergence insufficiency [1][2].
AAPOS states the behavioral aspects of vision therapy are scientifically unproven [5].
